transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-12-08 16:00 UTC | Duration: 46m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Amrita (Redwood SE), Samira (Redwood Partnerships); Carlos, Lena, Ibrahim, Maya (HelioCloud)

[00:00] Jordan Blake: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really quick intro — Jordan Blake from Redwood Inference, AE. Amrita is our solutions engineer, Samira on partnerships.
[00:08] Carlos Mendez: Hi all, Carlos here, head of partnerhsips at HelioCloud. Appreciate you taking the time.
[00:12] Amrita Singh: Hi Carlos, hi team, excited to chat through what a partner integration could look like. Quick agenda: goals, tech constraints, integration patterns, next steps.
[00:22] Lena Park: Sounds good — we're looking at two things: 1) offering Redwood-backed inference as an add-on in our marketplace, and 2) exploring wholesale GPU capacity for enterprise customers.
[00:33] Ibrahim Khan: Yeah we run a mix of A100 and H100 instances across regions, and curious about scheduling and how Redwood would place jobs on our fleet.
[00:41] Jordan Blake: Great, high level Redwood provides hosted API, dedicated reserved pools, and private deployments. For partners we typically do marketplace integrations or dedicated capacity with peering.
[00:51] Maya Torres: Security is a big one for us — what controls do you need? SSO, SAML, KMS, audit logs, and SOC 2 are table stakes for our customers.
[01:02] Amrita Singh: Absolutely — we support SAML/SSO, RBAC, customer-managed KMS/HSM for key control, and audit logs; we have a SOC 2 report we can share. For private deployments we can run a control plane in customer VPC or provide an air-gapped on-prem package.
[01:20] Ibrahim Khan: When you say private, do you mean Redwood runs your control plane in our VPC or you ship software we run?
[01:27] Amrita Singh: Both options — for the partner program we often recommend a hybrid: our control plane in a partner-managed VPC with peering, while the inference nodes can be in your tenant so data residency and keys stay you.
[01:40] Carlos Mendez: Ok makes sense — latency profiles matter for our gaming and streaming customers. What sort of p99 latency do you see on short-context chat workloads?
[01:50] Amrita Singh: On our hosted API p99 for common 8k token models is about 350ms for short prompts, but that varies by model and batch size. With dedicated pools on H100 and kernel tuning we can get lower tails — the tradeoff is cost and utilization.
[02:07] Jordan Blake: And we can route by policy — low-latency routes use reserved capacity; cheaper routes hit open-hosted or batched variants. For partners we can define SLA tiers.
[02:18] Lena Park: Do you support model variants/quantization? Some customers want int8 to save cost.
[02:24] Amrita Singh: Yes, we have quantization profiles and recommend model/quant policy based on workload. We also do KV cache and prefix caching which reduces token compute for repeated prompts.
[02:36] Ibrahim Khan: How do you handle multi-tenant on same GPU? We need isolation guarantees.
[02:41] Amrita Singh: For dedicated pools we provide tenant isolation via reserved instances and scheduling; for shared hosted we do namespace separation and strict RBAC. If HelioCloud wants a white-labeled managed offering we recommend dedicated reserved capacity per customer and optional hardware-level isolation.
[02:54] Carlos Mendez: From a commercial perspective, do you do revenue share on marketplace listings or referral fees?
[03:00] Jordan Blake: We can do both — early partners often start with referral fees and move to revenue-share or co-sell deals. We tailor to partner's GTM.
[03:08] Samira Ortiz: Quick Q: what's the cadence for support and SLOs on Dedicated?
[03:12] Amrita Singh: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and target latency, plus 24/7 support for enterprise tiers. We can include dedicated on-call and runbooks for escalation.
[03:21] Carlos Mendez: Nice. On the technical side, Ibrahim, can you share the GPU topologies? 1U pods, bare metal racks, network limits?
[03:28] Ibrahim Khan: Sure — majority are H100 80GB on RDMA fabric across 3 AZs; some A100 40GB in secondary regions. We do thin L2 peering and private link options. Bandwidth is 100GbE.
[03:40] Amrita Singh: That should be fine. Do you have constraints on outbound connectivity for our control plane? Some customers restrict control plane egress.
[03:48] Maya Torres: We do have stricter outbound rules for some enterprise tenants; we may need to host control plane inside our network for high-security customers.
[03:56] Amrita Singh: We can accommodate: air-gapped or customer-managed control plane options exist. We'll need to talk about updates/patching model then.
[04:06] Jordan Blake: A couple of potential integration patterns: (1) Marketplace listing — we host inference; you list Redwood product and handle billing; (2) Dedicated capacity — Redwood runs an orchestrator and scheduler with reserved GPU pools in HelioCloud tenancy; (3) Private deployment — Redwood software runs in your network and we do a managed install.
[04:23] Lena Park: For the dedicated capacity model, what telemetry do you need? We need to ensure we can export metrics to our monitoring stack.
[04:29] Amrita Singh: We support Prometheus endpoints, tracing hooks, per-route dashboards, and token-level cost/latency metrics. We also expose audit logs for compliance.
[04:40] Ibrahim Khan: Any concerns around kernel compatibility? We run mixed CUDA stacks.
[04:44] Amrita Singh: Our runtime selects kernels based on model arch and hardware. We typically validate on the target CUDA + driver stack; if there are custom kernels or proprietary drivers we'll need to run a short compatibility test.
[04:56] Jordan Blake: Also, we do a small benchmark harness — run a few representative prompts and measure p50/p95/p99 and throughput. That helps tune batching and quantization.
[05:06] Carlos Mendez: Good — we can provide a small sftp drop of model images and test prompts.
[05:11] Amrita Singh: Perfect. Quick note on security: for KMS we integrate with customer-managed KMS like AWS KMS or external HSMs; we can also support customer-provided keys in private deployments.
[05:23] Maya Torres: And audit logs — retention and access controls?
[05:26] Amrita Singh: Retention is configurable; we can ship logs to your SIEM and support role-based access to logs.
[05:33] Jordan Blake: Any blockers from a legal or procurement standpoint? Samira?
[05:36] Samira Ortiz: We'll need a standard MSA and potentially an addendum for marketplace revenue share. Also, HelioCloud might ask for an NDA early.
[05:44] Carlos Mendez: We'll send an NDA request. Procurement timeline is Q1 evaluation with pilot in late Jan.
[05:51] Jordan Blake: Sounds good. Proposed pilot: a small dedicated pool in one region for 6 weeks, run benchmarks and a joint go-to-market listing.
[05:59] Ibrahim Khan: For pilot we can commit 4 H100 instances for dedicated testing. Need to confirm scheduling and maintenance windows.
[06:07] Amrita Singh: We'll build an SLO/benchmark plan and share it. Jordan will follow up with integration doc.
[06:12] [Silence, typing]
[06:30] Jordan Blake: Quick question from me — do you have specific customers or verticals you'd prioritize?
[06:34] Lena Park: Telecom and gaming first, then enterprise ML platforms. Low-latency is key for gaming.
[06:40] Amrita Singh: Ok we'll focus on low-latency config for gaming workloads and show cost tradeoffs.
[06:47] Jordan Blake: Alright let's capture next steps.
[06:50] Carlos Mendez: One more security question — you mentioned SOC 2. Do you have any other certifications?
[06:55] Amrita Singh: We have SOC 2 in progress and roadmaps for ISO. For partner customers we can share interim compliance docs.
[07:03] Jordan Blake: Great. Anything else from the HelioCloud side?
[07:06] Ibrahim Khan: No, just that we'd like the benchmark harness and a quick script to run locally to validate network path.
[07:12] Amrita Singh: We'll provide a small benchmark harness repo and instructions.
[07:18] Jordan Blake: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with docs and set the infra deep-dive.
[07:23] Carlos Mendez: Thanks all.

[End of meeting]

Notes: transcription has occasional mis-hearings — e.g., partner names or product terms might be slightly off. The transcript captures the main flow and next steps.
